findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Structurally normal heart. Trace physiological mitral regurgitation.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait and distractibility, with entrainment during a witnessed event; reflexes and plantars normal
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Twelve months of fluctuating right leg weakness and shaking events: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and entrainment, and on the semiology of an observed event, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: She was given a diagnosis of psychogenic seizures elsewhere and doubts it. Recording her habitual events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty, re-examines the old label on positive evidence and assesses co-occurring epilepsy, as the AAN guideline advises. Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serotonergic overlap of escitalopram and as-needed sumatriptan; nothing on the list was started for the events
action_criteria.label: Review the current medicines for interactions
action_criteria.rationale: No antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine has been started for her events, so the review does not change the plan; the escitalopram and sumatriptan combination is worth noting.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lesion explaining the right leg weakness
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: Twelve months of progressive right leg weakness with sensory symptoms make a single non-contrast scan defensible, but symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, intact posterior column sensation and the positive signs already answer the structural question, so the scan does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her anxiety, mood and dissociative symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures and functional right leg weakness) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait, distractibility and entrainment, and on the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information. Address her doubt about the earlier label by going through the features of the events and the positive signs with her.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder, which has worsened since the separation.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: A head CT answers no question here: the right leg weakness and the events carry positive functional features, no sign points to a structural lesion, and the scan adds radiation and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
She is afebrile, alert and fully oriented, with no inflammatory or encephalopathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add iatrogenic risk and change nothing.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Midline-splitting, non-dermatomal light-touch loss with intact vibration and proprioception is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Recurrent shaking events with occasional reduced awareness. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

A syncope admission 6 months ago had an unrevealing cardiac work-up. The events last 30 seconds to 3 minutes with the eyes closed and retained responsiveness to voice, longer than syncopal jerking, and the recorded events kept a posterior alpha rhythm and sinus rhythm without a pause.

differential.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis or another structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Twelve months of fluctuating right leg weakness with sensory symptoms; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, normal tone, intact vibration and proprioception, and a positive Hoover sign with collapsing weakness are incompatible with a corticospinal or dorsal column lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait, distractibility and entrainment of the event shaking are validated rule-in signs; the midline-splitting sensory loss and variable pinprick boundaries are supportive only.

Two habitual events (bilateral arm shaking with the eyes closed, 1 min 40 s and 2 min 50 s) were recorded on video-EEG without ictal change, with a persisting posterior rhythm and a normal interictal record: the ILAE documented level of certainty.
An earlier diagnosis made elsewhere is re-examined on positive evidence; here the recorded events and the signs support it, and showing them to her is how her doubt is addressed.
The prior syncope admission had an unrevealing cardiac work-up, and the long events with closed eyes and preserved responsiveness are not syncopal; the cardiac tests need not be repeated.
The separation, financial stress and generalized anxiety disorder are supportive context; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder diagnosed 4 years ago, worse over the past 3 months
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Separation from her partner 3 months ago and financial difficulties
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressor alone, without positive signs or typical event semiology

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A prior diagnosis is re-examined on positive evidence: the examination signs and the event semiology, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, not the earlier label, establish the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Psychogenic seizures diagnosed at an outside facility during the current illness, a label she doubts
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the outside label without examining her and recording the events, or, given her doubt, discard it and restart an epilepsy work-up

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The cardiac work-up was unrevealing, and events lasting up to 3 minutes with closed eyes and preserved responsiveness are not syncopal; repeating it answers no new question.
red_herrings.data_point: Hospitalization for syncope 6 months ago with an unrevealing cardiac work-up
red_herrings.intended_effect: Repeat the ECG, Holter monitoring and echocardiography to look for convulsive syncope

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right leg strength gives way abruptly on direct testing, rated 4-/5.
Right leg dragged behind on walking; the gait normalizes transiently when she is distracted by conversation.
Right heel-to-shin normal when her attention is diverted, effortful on direct testing.
During the witnessed event the arm shaking took up the slower rhythm she was asked to tap with her right foot.
Bilateral upper limb shaking of varying frequency with the eyes closed for about 90 seconds, followed by rapid recovery without confusion, tongue biting or incontinence.

Non-dermatomal light-touch loss over the whole right leg with a midline split, variable pinprick boundaries, normal use of the leg when not formally tested and exaggerated Romberg sway without falling; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric with flexor plantars and no clonus; normal tone; vibration and proprioception intact.
findings.sign: Reflexes, tone and posterior column sensation

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility of the right leg deficit, with entrainment of the shaking during the witnessed event. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed, bilateral shaking of varying frequency, entrainment, rapid recovery without confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Escitalopram with sumatriptan: additive serotonergic effect. Serotonin syndrome is rare with this combination; warn about agitation, tremor, hyperthermia and myoclonus, particularly after repeated triptan doses.
current_medications.proposed: Escitalopram 10 mg once daily; sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine; loperamide 2 mg as needed
current_medications.summary: One moderate serotonergic interaction (escitalopram with sumatriptan); no other clinically significant interactions among the current medicines.
warnings: Escitalopram: dose-dependent QTc prolongation; avoid adding other QT-prolonging drugs.
Loperamide: QT prolongation and arrhythmia have been reported only at doses far above the labelled maximum; no interaction at 2 mg as needed.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes. No epileptiform abnormalities provoked. No habitual event triggered.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Performed at standard frequencies (1-30 Hz). Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: Present during both events; the background remained interpretable between bursts.

background.overall: Continuous inpatient video-EEG for 48 hours, international 10-20 system with a single-lead ECG channel. Normal, symmetric background in wakefulness and sleep.
background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, well-regulated, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture; vertex waves and sleep spindles in stage N2 sleep

findings.morphology: Bilateral upper limb shaking of varying frequency and amplitude with the eyes closed, lasting 1 min 40 s. Movement artifact over the frontal and temporal channels; the posterior alpha rhythm remained visible between artifact bursts. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

Bilateral arm shaking spreading to the trunk with the eyes closed, lasting 2 min 50 s; she answered the technologist by name midway through the event. Posterior alpha rhythm persisted throughout; no evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.
Sinus rhythm throughout the recording; rate rose from 82 to 112/min during the events, with no pause or arrhythmia.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Two habitual events were recorded (bilateral upper limb shaking with the eyes closed, 1 min 40 s and 2 min 50 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement and muscle artifact briefly obscured the frontal and temporal channels during the events.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case: positive signs of functional right leg weakness, a witnessed event with functional semiology, and habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change. The patient doubts an outside label of psychogenic seizures and had an earlier syncope admission.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination; a video-EEG can confirm the events. The outside label invites either uncritical acceptance or a fresh epilepsy work-up, and the old syncope admission invites repeat cardiac testing; the main task is explaining the diagnosis to a patient who doubts it.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: policy tiers, reports and assessment rebuilt to the FND condition plan. Close-out 24 Oct 2026: video-EEG optional and red-flag tests recommended, per the July 2026 agreement with the physicians that the examination is the only required diagnostic act.

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of shaking and right leg weakness for the past 12 months

family_history: Mother with generalized anxiety disorder and fibromyalgia
No family history of epilepsy, stroke, or cardiac disease
past_medical_history: Generalized anxiety disorder, diagnosed 4 years ago
Migraine without aura, episodic, since age 18
History of psychogenic seizures diagnosed at an outside facility during the current illness
One prior hospitalization for syncope 6 months ago, cardiac workup unrevealing

social_history.recent_stressors: Recently separated from long-term partner 3 months ago; experiencing financial difficulties

patient.history_present_illness: A 26-year-old right-handed woman presents to the neurology inpatient service with a 12-month history of recurrent episodes of shaking and subjective right leg weakness. The episodes began approximately one year ago and have been increasing in frequency, now occurring several times per week. Each episode consists of bilateral upper extremity tremor, sometimes progressing to whole-body shaking, lasting between 30 seconds and 3 minutes. She reports that the episodes are sometimes preceded by a sense of anxiety or lightheadedness, but often occur without clear warning. She occasionally loses awareness during the events, though bystanders report that she appears to respond to voice during some episodes. She has not sustained injuries during these events and denies tongue-biting or urinary incontinence. Between episodes, she has noticed progressive weakness of her right leg, which she describes as a heaviness and difficulty lifting the limb. The weakness fluctuates throughout the day and is sometimes worse with stress. She reports that the right leg occasionally gives way, causing her to stumble, though she has not fallen. She also describes intermittent decreased sensation over the right leg. Three months ago, she separated from her long-term partner and has been under significant financial stress. Her anxiety has worsened over this period. She was previously told at an outside hospital that she had psychogenic seizures, but she is uncertain about this diagnosis and seeks further evaluation. She denies fevers, weight loss, visual changes, dysphagia, or bowel or bladder dysfunction.

neurological_exam.additional: During examination, patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking with eye closure lasting approximately 90 seconds. The shaking varied in frequency and was entrained: its rhythm changed to match a slower rhythm she was asked to tap with her right foot. No post-event confusion. No tongue-biting. No incontinence.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin intact on the left. On the right, performance is inconsistent — normal on distraction but effortful on direct testing.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II-XII intact. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. No nystagmus. Facial sensation and strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Demonstrates dragging of the right leg with inconsistent pattern. When distracted by conversation, gait normalizes transiently. No Trendelenburg sign. Romberg test shows dramatic swaying without falling, with self-correction.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect mildly anxious but cooperative. Speech fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Attention and concentration intact. Memory intact for immediate, short-term, and long-term recall.
neurological_exam.motor: Right lower extremity demonstrates give-way weakness with 4-/5 strength on direct testing but observed to use the limb normally when not being formally tested. Left lower extremity 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities 5/5 bilaterally. Normal bulk and tone throughout. Hoover sign positive on the right: right hip extension is weak on direct testing but becomes full when she flexes the left hip against resistance.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric throughout upper and lower extremities. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch over the entire right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution with a sharp midline split. Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally. Pin prick testing inconsistent with repeat examinations showing variable boundaries.
